The notes are discrete overtones, and the fundamental and second overtone are hard to excite, so a beginner should first keep a steady rate of spin and then practise steps of speed. The blown version needs a narrower bore, and the tongue and throat can interrupt the airflow to skip overtones. For concert use the tube must be trimmed to tune it.

In 1973 Frank Crawford noted that toys of this kind had appeared in toy shops a year or two earlier and studied their acoustics; he developed the corrugahorn, a blown version of the small corrugated tube. For concert use the tube must be trimmed to tune it. David Cope discussed the cugaphone in 1972, and in 1997 described a version made of a trumpet mouthpiece, plastic tubing and a funnel. Roderic Knight proposed a revised classification, the whirled version as A21.31 and the blown version as A21.32.
雷鳴管音色深沉渾厚，具有戲劇性的音響效果。其獨特的音色質感介於金屬與木質之間，帶: The thunder tube has a deep, full timbre with a dramatic effect. Its particular colour falls between metal and wood, dark and mysterious. The instrument makes a low rumble by plucking or shaking the spring, its range sits in the low to low-middle register, and it can produce a convincing roll of thunder. The way it resonates is unusual: the body itself vibrates in several layers, so the sound is constantly changing. Where a traditional percussion instrument such as a drum or gong is crisp and clean, the thunder tube is more penetrating and enveloping; beside the bass of a piano its sound is more metallic and more modern. This expressive timbre makes it a natural choice for film scores, sound design and modern composition.

The thunder tube (whirly tube, corrugaphone, once sold as Free-Ka) is an experimental instrument made from a corrugated plastic tube or hose, open at both ends, one of which may be wider. The player holds one end and whirls the other in a circle, so that the air flowing over the corrugations makes vortices; the faster it is whirled, the higher the pitch, and the pitches follow the overtone series roughly. It is an aerophone, Hornbostel–Sachs 412.22, but it is often put with the percussion sound effects. Street sellers in New York City sold it in the late 1960s; it has also been used in Peter Brooks's production of A Midsummer Night's Dream, by various artists, in marching bands and in performances at the University of Michigan.
